newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Senate gives rubber tappers a boost.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Senate gives rubber tappers a boost.

text.p: Defenders of Brazil's struggling rubber tappers claimed a victory on Tuesday when the Senate approved a bill creating subsidies for rubber producers, with extra for those in the Amazon rain forest.
The bill will become law only if the lower house of Congress, which has already approved the legislation, goes along with changes in the text made by the Senate.
But Sen. Marina Silva, who grew up as a rubber tapper in the remote Amazonian state of Acre, said the legislation represented a major boost for the region.
"This is one of the most important contributions any government has made for the rubber industry in the last 30 years," Silva, a member of the left-wing opposition Workers Party, said.
The bill creates subsidies of up to 38 cents per pound (83 cents per kg) for rubber produced in Brazil, enough to make the product of industrial groves competitive with imports from Asia.

Rubber tappers in the Amazon, who milk trees that grow naturally in the forest and who have been hardest hit by foreign competition, qualify for an additional subsidy to make up for the difficulties of getting their rubber to market.

"These people often have to carry their harvests for two hours on their backs and then for several more hours by boat before they even reach a road," Silva said. "The rule of the market cannot be applied to them."

Unlike the industrial growers, whose subsidies will be gradually reduced over eight years, the Amazon rubber tappers will be entitled to financial support for as long as it takes the government to invest in transportation and cooperatives.

Brazil was once the world's largest producer of rubber, and proceeds from the crop helped build Manaus and Belem, the biggest cities in the Amazon. But the introduction of industrial groves in Asia transformed the industry and ruined Brazilian growers.

Small communities continued to tap rubber trees in the forest, selling their product to Brazilian tire manufacturers, before the lowering of import tariffs prompted a flood of foreign rubber onto the Brazilian market.

An estimated 70,000 families depend on rubber tapping in the Amazon, down from 300,000 in the 1970s, an aide to Silva said. Many earn little more than $50 a month and survive by hunting, fishing and in some cases illegally selling precious timber in their reserves, he said.
